summary:
Odyssey Outpost is a free, browser-based 2D survival trainer for junior astronauts, built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. You are the last person at a Mars or Moon outpost and must survive 14 sols or days. You manage oxygen, water, food, power, health and suit air while doing real tasks: cleaning solar panels, growing crops, drilling for water ice, swapping CO2 filters and fixing leaks. Every job costs time. Four missions, random events like dust storms and solar flares, and a mission report keep each run different.

It answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by teaching calm decision-making under pressure. Safety checks come before risky jobs, such as lockout before touching moving equipment. After every result, a “Why?” button explains what happened with a simplified NASA fact, and the NASA sources are listed in the game.

This matters because future space missions need people who think safely when things go wrong. Odyssey Outpost makes those habits fun, short and accessible on any device, including phones, for young learners.
details:
What it does and how it works
Odyssey Outpost is a 2D survival trainer that runs in the browser. The player is alone at a Mars or Moon outpost for 14 sols or days. They walk the base with the keyboard, mouse or touch buttons, stand on a glowing pad and choose a task. Tasks include cleaning solar panels, growing and harvesting crops, drilling for water ice, swapping CO2 filters, fixing leaks and realigning the antenna. Meters track oxygen, water, food, power, health and suit air. Walking, suiting up and repairs all use hours, so time is a resource. Sleeping in Crew Quarters ends the day, and things change overnight. Random events such as dust storms, leaks, solar flares, moonquakes and power faults test the player, and Mission Control gives forecasts and a "Next step" hint. There are four missions: Mars Base Duty, Mars: Left Behind, Moon Base Duty and Moon: The Long Night. Each run ends with a mission report showing a score, a rank and what the player faced and learned.

Benefits and intended impact
Young learners practise staying calm and choosing safely. Quick safety checks come before risky jobs, for example lockout before touching moving equipment. After any success, failure, alert or blocked action, a "Why?" button explains the result with a simplified NASA fact. The aim is to build safe habits and curiosity about space missions, with short text that is easy to read.

Tools and technology
We used HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no libraries. Graphics are drawn on an HTML canvas. Music and sound effects are generated in the browser with the Web Audio API, so there are no audio files. The code is split into data (missions, events, tasks, NASA sources), audio, rendering and game logic. We developed it in VS Code and host it on GitHub Pages, so it needs no install.

Creativity
We mixed two ideas: the long, obstacle-filled journey of Odysseus and the "left behind" survival of The Martian. The game uses time as the main currency, so every choice has a cost. The explanation after every result turns mistakes into lessons. The look is cartoonish but serious, with a navy and black space theme and synthesized music.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: Facts are simplified from public NASA information, and the in-game "NASA sources" button lists them. The game does not download live data.
  • Honesty: It is labelled an educational prototype, not an official NASA product or real mission guidance.
  • Accessibility: It works with keyboard, mouse and touch, and the text is short and simple for young learners.
